title: Half of us fear how AI is used
full_text:
Australians are demanding stronger rules for artificial intelligence companies amid growing fears about AI-generated misinformation, cybercrime and privacy risks, as new research reveals half of Aussies think the dangers outweigh the benefits of the tech.
The Andrew “Twiggy” Forrest-backed SafeAI initiative polled 2300 Australians, finding an even 50 per cent now believe the risks of AI outweigh the benefits, up from 46 per cent at the same time last year.
Fewer than a third – 32 per cent – think the opposite.
AI-generated misinformation and disinformation, and criminal misuse and cybercrime are equal top concerns, but even the lowest-ranked fears, such as the risk of AI becoming conscious and ending humanity, are still moderately or very concerning for 76 per cent of those surveyed.
Most Australians want the government to step in with a “balanced” approach to regulating AI, the SafeAI research found, but an increasing proportion now favour “strict rules that limit risk, even if it slows innovation”, up from 28 per cent in August 2025 to 39 per cent in September.
Minderoo Foundation campaigns director Sam Calabrese said Australians wanted to “trust that someone has their hand on the steering wheel, when it comes to AI safety”, and getting it right would “unlock permission from the public to really make the most of … AI”. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese on Tuesday outlined some of the measures his government intended to enact, including establishing an AI regulator that would be able to penalise AI companies that failed to comply with safety obligations.
Minderoo’s Mr Calabrese said: “We want to see how that rolls out and works practically, (including) what sort of resourcing they’re going to need to successfully deliver that.” Frontier AI labs would also be required to allow independent evaluation of their models, under the proposed Australian standards, and notify the Australian government “rapidly” about any incidents.
In September, ChatGPT creator OpenAI was forced to apologise to the Australian public for failing to notice for months that its bots had hacked a Medicare statistics portal, and informing Services Australia using a public mailbox. The incident sparked a rapid review involving several government agencies, which recommended “mandatory, time-bound” reporting for rogue AI actions, and that the government consider making “failure to prevent” harm a stand-alone criminal offence.
Mr Albanese said further details of the government’s legislative response would be announced in due course, but some in the industry have already expressed scepticism about the planned standards.
The Australian Computer Society warned professional expertise in AI was lacking in critical public systems. Monash University cybersecurity lecturer Dr Chetan Arora said while the proposals were a “good first step”, more needed to be done to prevent rogue AI incidents from occurring in the first place.
